profile.reading:
Bloomberg LP's data center at 155 Corporate Drive in Orangeburg, in the town of Orangetown, Rockland County, sits on a former Verizon owned property that developer Russo Development Corporation bought in 2009 and redeveloped for data center use, partnering with Sentinel Data Centers on the build out. Bloomberg signed its lease in May 2013 for a 131,806 square foot building, with Orangetown's town council approving a resolution on May 14, the Pearl River school district's board approving its share of the arrangement on May 21, and Supervisor Andy Stewart authorized to sign a twelve year payment in lieu of taxes agreement shortly after, with the Rockland County Industrial Development Agency also endorsing the deal. Bloomberg's own head of research at the time was quoted saying the site checked every box the company needed, and trade press reporting from the period put the scale of investment at up to 710 million dollars over roughly fifteen years, including an initial 435 million dollars for renovation and fit out, with the facility targeted to open by mid 2014.

The site's attraction was largely electrical. Trade press coverage described up to four 13 kilovolt circuits feeding the building, each rated for up to 10 megawatts, for a stated total utility capacity of 40 megawatts, fed by subterranean 138 kilovolt transmission lines in a ring bus configuration tied to an adjacent substation, a configuration chosen for the redundancy financial data infrastructure requires and for the site's proximity to the New York Stock Exchange's own data hub roughly 25 miles south. New York's Department of Environmental Conservation issued Bloomberg LP an air facility permit, effective January 2, 2024 and running through January 1, 2034, covering up to eight emergency generators, capping combined annual generator run time at 949 hours and total nitrogen oxide emissions at 49,500 pounds a year, which stands as the clearest public, dated record of the facility's backup generation footprint even though it states an emissions ceiling rather than a generator megawatt rating directly.

That 40 megawatt utility figure and the DEC's generator count describe different things, utility delivered power and standby emergency capacity, and neither is a stated critical IT load, which was not found in any source reviewed for this entry. Rockland County has more recently become a flashpoint in state level data center policy debate, including reporting on a large tax break tied to a separate JPMorgan facility in the county and discussion of a statewide moratorium in 2026, but no source found in this research ties that newer controversy specifically to the Bloomberg site, which has operated under its original 2013 payment in lieu of taxes arrangement for well over a decade with comparatively little public friction.
profile.research_note: Address (155 Corporate Drive, Orangeburg NY 10962) confirmed against NY DEC air facility permit 3-3924-00434/00002, an official government primary source, exact match to OSM housenumber/street tags. 40 MW figure is utility circuit capacity per DatacenterKnowledge trade press (2013 announcement), not confirmed as still current in 2026. Generator count (up to eight) and 949 hour/year runtime cap and NOx cap are from the DEC permit effective through Jan 2034, useful as standby generation context but permit gives no per-generator MW rating.

reading.body:
Bloomberg's Orangeburg data center sits on 143,331 square feet in Rockland County, New York, with utility circuits rated for 40 megawatts total capacity fed by redundant 138 kilovolt transmission lines to an adjacent substation. The site was engineered for the electrical redundancy that financial data infrastructure requires, positioned 25 miles north of the New York Stock Exchange's own data hub. No critical IT load figure is published for the facility.

The 40 megawatt utility capacity figure dates to the 2013 lease announcement and is not confirmed current as of 2026. The facility's published specifications do not state how much of that utility capacity is in active use. A New York Department of Environmental Conservation air permit effective through January 2034 authorizes up to eight emergency generators with a combined annual runtime capped at 949 hours and nitrogen oxide emissions capped at 49,500 pounds per year, but the permit does not specify individual generator ratings in megawatts. The two figures describe different things: utility delivered power and standby emergency generation.

Within New York State, 31 data center facilities are mapped, but only two operators publish megawatt figures for sites reviewed by this research. Bloomberg's 40 megawatts ranks second in the state by published capacity. Rockland County became a flashpoint in state-level data center policy debate after 2013, including reporting on a separate JPMorgan facility's tax arrangement and discussion of a statewide moratorium in 2026, but no source found ties that newer controversy to the Bloomberg site, which has operated under its original twelve-year payment in lieu of taxes agreement since 2013 with comparatively minimal public friction.
